Chat is improvisation. When work has to run the same way every time, you write it down as a workflow: a <sub alias='yammel'>YAML</sub> file of nodes, where depends on draws the edges between them. Keelson reads the file as a graph, and runs it in that order, every time.
n2: Here's one for the harbor repo: run the tests, print the tides, then have an agent report on both. The last line points at a node called tide. There isn't one.
n3: Validate runs the same loader the server uses, and it names the problem before anything runs.
n4: That's why you validate first. The loader checks that every edge lands on a real node, every output a prompt reads comes from one, and there are no cycles. An unknown field is only a warning. But a broken edge found at run time would stop the run halfway, after earlier steps had already done their work.
n5: Add the missing letter, save, and validate again.
n7: Now run it. Test and tides depend on nothing, so they start together. Report waits for both, and their output is wired into its prompt.
n8: In the browser, the run is the same graph. The report read the two results it was handed, and kept the time exactly as printed.
n9: So a workflow is a file you can read, a graph Keelson can check, and a run that goes the same way every time. Chat leaves the control flow to the model. A workflow takes it back, and hands the model only the steps that need one.
n10: Write it, check it, run it.
n11: Keelson. Lay the keel, raise the ribs.
